36#main: One row planted on the ground and one row on a step—if the step is higher than the ground by ten handbreadths they do not combine; less than this—they combine.
37#main: One who plants five vines—two corresponding to two and one protruding a tail—behold this is called a small vineyard and he must distance from them four amot in every direction. But if he planted two corresponding to two and one in the middle, or three in a row and two opposite them in a second row—they are not a vineyard and he distances from them only six handbreadths in every direction.
38#main: A ruined vineyard—if in it there are ten vines to harvest per se'ah of land, planted two corresponding to two and one protruding a tail, or if in it there are three corresponding to three—behold it is called a poor vineyard and it is forbidden to sow in all of it.
39#main: A vineyard not planted in rows but mixed—if in it there are three corresponding to two, behold it is a vineyard; and if not, it is not a vineyard but suffices to distance six handbreadths from each vine and vine and sow.
40#main: If the trunks were aligned and the foliage was not aligned, behold it is a vineyard; if the foliage was aligned and the trunks were not aligned, it is not a vineyard. If they were thin and not aligned, but the thick ones are aligned—behold it is a vineyard.
41#main: How does one know if they are aligned? He brings a measuring cord and stretches from one to another.
42#main: A vineyard ruined in its middle and intact on all its sides around—if in the bald patch in the middle there are sixteen amot, behold he distances four amot in every direction from the roots of the vines and sows in the middle of the bald patch; and if there are not sixteen amot in it, behold he does not bring seed there. And if he brought, since he distanced four amot in every direction from the vines of the vineyard, behold he did not cause hikdish.
43#main: And likewise a place left empty without vines between the end of the vineyard and its fence—and this is called the vineyard's bald area—if in it there are twelve amot, he distances four amot from the vines and sows the remainder. If in it there were less than twelve amot, he does not bring seed there. And if he brought, since he distanced four amot, behold he did not cause hikdish. In what case is this said? In a large vineyard; but in a small one it has no bald area except that he distances four amot from the end of the vines and sows until the fence. And likewise a large vineyard that had between each row and row eight amot or more has no bald area.
44#main: If the fence surrounding the vineyard was less than ten handbreadths high, or if its height was ten handbreadths but it does not have a width of four handbreadths, it has no bald area except that he distances four amot from the end of the vines and sows until the partition—even if between the vines and the partition there were four and a half amot, he sows half an amah.
45#main: A fence that is ten handbreadths high, and likewise a ditch that is ten handbreadths deep and four handbreadths wide—behold it is permitted to plant a vineyard on this side and vegetables on that side, even a partition of reeds—if between reed and fellow there are not three handbreadths, behold it separates between vineyard and vegetable like a fence.
46#main: A fence separating between vineyard and vegetable that was breached up to ten amot—behold it is like an opening and permitted. If it was breached more than ten, opposite the breach it is forbidden until he distances from the vines according to the measure of the breach. If many breaches were made in it—if the standing portion is like the breached, behold it is permitted as though there is no breach there. If the breach exceeded the standing, he does not sow opposite all the breached places until he distances according to the measure.
47#main: A vineyard partition that was breached—they tell him: fence it. A breach—they tell him: fence it. If he despaired of it and did not fence it, behold he has caused hikdish.
48#main: A house half roofed and half not roofed, and vines planted on this side—it is permitted to sow vegetables on the other side, for the mouth of the roof is as though it descended and closed, and between them it becomes like a partition. And if he made the roofing even, it is forbidden.
49#main: A small courtyard breached in its entirety into a large one, and the vines were in the large one—it is forbidden to sow in the small one; and if he sowed, the seeds are forbidden and the vines permitted. If the vines were in the small one, it is permitted to sow in the large one, since in the large one there are partitions on this side and that side—behold it is like separated from the small one, and the small one is not separated from the large one.
50#main: A ditch passing through a vineyard, ten deep and four wide—if it was open from the head of the vineyard to its end, behold it is viewed as between two vineyards and permitted to sow within it, provided the vines do not provide covering over it. And if it was not open, behold it is like a winepress in the middle of the vineyard—for even though it is ten deep and four wide or more, it is forbidden to sow within it unless in the bald patch there were sixteen amot.
51#main: A path between two vineyards—behold it is like a vineyard ruined in its middle: if between them there are sixteen amot, he distances from this one four amot and from that one four amot and sows the remainder; and if there were less than this, he does not bring seed there.
52#main: A watchman's hut (meaning: a dwelling house made for the field watchman) in a vineyard—if it is ten high and four wide, it is permitted to sow vegetable on its roof, provided the tendrils do not touch it so that vegetable does not appear inside the vineyard from above. In what case is this said? When it is square; but if the watchman's hut was round, it needs a hollow of four handbreadths within so that it is prominent from the ground, and it needs earth on its roof from above three handbreadths.
53#main: A house in a vineyard—if it is more than three handbreadths by three handbreadths, they sow vegetable inside it; and if it is less than three by three, behold it is closed and they do not sow inside it.
54#main: A single vine planted in a valley or in a ditch—he distances six handbreadths in every direction and sows the whole ditch as he does on level ground. And if it was ten deep and the lip of the ditch above was four wide, it is forbidden to sow within it even though he distanced six.
55#main: And likewise a single vine surrounded by a fence ten high and four wide—he does not sow in the whole partition even though he distanced six. And if he distanced six and sowed, he did not cause hikdish. And how much should he distance initially and sow? Four amot in every direction, and afterward he sows the rest of the ditch or the rest of the place surrounded by fence.
56#main: Vines that grew in their natural state and behold their tendrils and clusters are cast on the ground—these are called a vineyard. But one who makes like a bed or like a high bench (meaning: raised) above the ground so that clusters and tendrils spread upon it, and he raised the vine's foliage above the ground upon that bed and suspended them—behold this is called an aris (trellis). And those reeds and the like from which he made a bed or bench and suspended upon them the vine's foliage—these are called a trellis (afifirah), and there are other laws for an aris.
57#main: One who plants one row of five vines or more and trellised them on a wall ten high and the like, or planted them beside a ditch ten deep and four wide—behold these are called an aris and he must distance from the aris four amot and afterward sow as he distances from a vineyard. And from where does one measure? From the root of the fence on which he trellised them.
58#main: How so? If he distanced the row of vines from the wall one amah and the aris from the vines is found, and to the wall—he measures from the wall four amot and sows, and between the seed and the roots of the vines five amot are found. And if he comes to sow from the side of the vines, he distances four amot from the roots of the vines and finds five amot distant from the wall. And on this manner we judge every aris.
59#main: Whether one builds the fence and afterward plants, or plants and afterward makes the fence—since he trellised them, behold it is an aris. If the fence was destroyed or the ditch was stopped up, there is no aris here but behold the whole row is like individual vines.
60#main: An aris ruined in its middle and five vines remained on the side of the fence on this side and five vines on the side of the other fence opposite them—this is called broken sections of an aris: if between them there are eight amot, and one of sixty per amah, behold he distances from each row six handbreadths and sows, provided he does not sow under the trellis. If between them there were eight amot precisely, behold he does not sow there. And if he sowed, since he distanced from each row six handbreadths, behold he did not cause hikdish. And if there is no fence there, he distances from each row sixteen handbreadths and sows, for there is neither aris nor broken sections of aris. If he returned and built the fence, the aris returned to its place and the broken sections of aris returned to their place.
61#main: A small garden surrounded by a fence and he trellised the vines around it outside on all its walls—if in it there is full harvesting and a basket from here and full harvesting and a basket from there, since it is surrounded by a fence they sow vegetables inside it. And if it does not have this measure, they do not sow inside it because everything appears like one aris with vegetable inside it.
62#main: Vines planted on a high step and its aris emerges and provides covering over the field—if he stands on the ground and harvests all of it, we view the whole place under the aris as though it were the place of the roots of the vines and forbid four amot in the field in every direction from the edge of the aris. And if he cannot harvest until he ascends the step or a ladder, it is forbidden to sow only under the aris alone.
63#main: Two walls adjacent one to the other and vines planted in the corners between them and the aris emerges with the walls from the corner and ends—he distances from the roots of the vines according to the measure and sows in the place of the end where there is no aris upon it, even though the seed is aligned between the two walls between which is the aris—since he distanced according to the measure, behold he sows between the walls.
64#main: A vine whose tree emerged a little from the ground and afterward bent and spread on the ground and rose again like a knee (meaning: like a bent human leg resembling a nun)—when measuring between seed and vine six handbreadths or four amot, one measures only from the end of the knee and not from the first root of the vine.
65#main: It has already been explained that even though he distances between seed and vine according to the measure, he must be careful that the vine does not provide covering over the vegetable nor the vegetable over the vine.
66#main: One sowed vegetable or grain seed and it grew and afterward he roofed the vine over it—the straw is permitted and the grain is burned.
67#main: If the roots of the vine extended into the four amot between the vineyard and the grain, he uproots. If the roots of the grain extended into the four amot, it is permitted.
68#main: All the distancing and measures stated in kilayim are with an amah of six handbreadths, ground.
69#main: All these measures that one distances between vines and grain or vegetable apply only in Eretz Yisrael or Syria; but in the Diaspora it is permitted to sow initially beside vines within the vineyard. And they forbade in the Diaspora only to sow two species of vegetable or two species of grain with vine seed casually. And if he told a non-Jewish child to sow for him in the Diaspora, it is permitted; but he may not tell an adult non-Jew lest it be confused with an Israelite. And even though it is permitted to sow vegetable beside the vineyard in the Diaspora, behold that vegetable sown there is forbidden in eating even in the Diaspora—when one sees him harvest and sell; but its doubt is permitted. {Rama: And some say that since it is permitted to sow vegetable beside vines in the Diaspora, it is permitted to eat that vegetable as well (Hagahot Maimoniyos chapter 10 of Ma'achalot Assurot law 9 and Terumat HaDeshen siman 194). And one should be concerned only in a place where there is reason to fear they were sown as two species of vegetable or two species of grain with vine seed casually (Mordechai on the first chapter of Kiddushin). Therefore they are accustomed to be lenient in these lands with vegetables found sown in vineyards, for it is not common that they were sown in prohibition.}
